Le calvaire que vivent les demandeurs d’: The ordeal asylum seekers face when they fall ill
La vulnérabilité des demandeurs d’asile: Asylum seekers’ vulnerability is not limited to the worlds of employment or housing. For some, falling ill can be a nightmare.
Giuliana et sa famille sont arrivées au: Giuliana and her family arrived in Canada via Roxham Road in October 2022. Photo: María Gabriela Aguzzi
La vulnérabilité des demandeurs d’asile: The vulnerability of asylum seekers in Canada, and in Quebec, goes beyond the difficulty of finding housing, a job or a daycare spot for their children. Nor is it limited to waiting for a work permit that will get them out of exploitation, which too often means working under the table. For these immigrants, falling ill can become a nightmare. And yet, once their asylum claim process has begun, they have, in theory, access to medical services.
Les demandeurs d’asile, qui, selon Stati: Asylum seekers, who numbered some 176,000 as of January 1<sup>st</sup>, 2024, according to Statistics Canada, do in fact have access to the <l1>Interim Federal Health Program (IFHP)</l1>, designed to cover some of their medical needs. These immigrants access health services through the insurance company Blue Cross, which means that doctors and other health care providers bill the insurer for their services each time they see an asylum seeker.
C’est la fameuse feuille brune, officiel: It is the famous brown sheet, officially the <l1>Refugee Protection Claimant Document (RPCD)</l1>, that gives them access to services in hospitals.
Cette couverture leur permet de s’adress: This coverage allows them to see other health professionals, including for prenatal and postnatal care. It also guarantees access to clinical psychologists, psychotherapists, occupational therapists, speech-language pathologists and physiotherapists, among others.
Bien que l’accès aux services médicaux s: Although access to medical services seems well organized, at least in theory, the path for an asylum seeker who wants to get health care in a timely manner is often long and arduous, even though doctors are not allowed to turn away asylum-seeking patients. “Many clinics do it, and the Collège des médecins du Québec does not monitor this practice,” says Juan Carlos Chirgwin, a family doctor in Parc-Extension, the most densely populated neighbourhood in Montréal – and one of the most diverse.
Le médecin de famille reconnaît que « le: The family doctor acknowledges that “things have improved over the past five years, but there is still no follow-up on what is happening on the ground in each clinic.”
Le parcours de ces migrants est semé d’e: These migrants’ journey is full of pitfalls. Language is the first obstacle. While information about the Interim Federal Health Program (IFHP) is easily found on the Internet, it is available only in French and English on the Canadian government’s official websites.
« Je travaille au CLSC de Parc-Extension: “I work at the CLSC in Parc-Extension, a neighbourhood where newcomers are the majority. There are a lot of asylum seekers, but also immigrants with other statuses. Many of them speak only their mother tongue. These are people who face a very significant language barrier,” says D<sup>r</sup>. Chirgwin.
Devant un tel obstacle, les demandeurs d: Faced with such an obstacle, asylum seekers often turn to their own community, which then becomes a basic source of information for newcomers.
« Dans de nombreux cas, l’information es: “In many cases, information is passed along by word of mouth,” says the family doctor. And this is despite the existence of the Programme régional d’accueil et d’intégration des demandeurs d’asile (PRAIDA), whose mandate and obligation is to inform them about the services they can benefit from and how to access them.
Pourtant, les demandeurs d’asile au Québ: Yet not all asylum seekers in Quebec are in contact with the agency, as Dr. Chirgwin has seen in Parc-Extension. Those who arrive in Canada by plane and then claim asylum, for example, are not necessarily directed to this service.
« Trente pour cent des demandeurs d’asil: “Thirty per cent of the asylum seekers I saw in 2018 and 2019 had no idea what PRAIDA was. They didn’t know how to access clinics; they didn’t know what the brown sheet was, let alone that it gave them access to physiotherapy and psychology services, as well as some dental and vision care,” says Juan Carlos Chirgwin.
Ce programme dispose d’informations bien: The program has detailed information for asylum seekers on its website, but the content is available only in English and French. Basic information about PRAIDA in Spanish, Arabic, Creole and Turkish is, however, available on <l1>the website of the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR)</l1>.
Nous avons consulté le PRAIDA pour conna: We consulted PRAIDA to get its perspective on language barriers. According to Barry Morgan, the program’s communications officer, “there is no particular approach regarding language access to medical services, other than encouraging allophone users to be accompanied by someone when booking appointments. Internally, within PRAIDA, users always have access to an interpretation service, as needed.”
Le CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Mo: The CIUSSS du Centre-Ouest-de-l’Île-de-Montréal, the institution that PRAIDA is part of, strives to “facilitate access by offering remote interpretation services that are available almost instantly (video or telephone) through Voyce,” adds Mr. Barry.
Les obstacles linguistiques s’étendent m: Language barriers even extend to the solutions adopted by the government to try to improve the health care system for the general public. These are measures that should, in principle, make access to health care easier for asylum seekers.
« Nous avons maintenant le Guichet d’acc: “We now have the Guichet d’accès à la première ligne (Primary Care Access Point), which connects a patient to a clinic, but not to a specific doctor. You can access this system by calling 811, option 3. Someone will ask the sick person questions and can sometimes refer them to a clinic for a one-time appointment. If the person gets sick again, they can call 811 again and be redirected, perhaps to a different clinic,” explains Juan Carlos Chirgwin.
Mais que se passe-t-il si une personne q: But what happens if a person who speaks neither French nor English calls 811 and explains their need? “Interpreters were promised, but I haven’t yet tried calling and speaking only in Spanish to see what happens.”
Au cours d’un test que nous avons effect: In a test we conducted, the 811 operator told us that “unfortunately, they did not have an interpreter and could only provide assistance in French or English to guide the patient to a medical service.” We were nonetheless told that an asylum seeker who speaks neither French nor English can call with the help of a friend acting as an interpreter.
Maira Prado, physiothérapeute à la Clini: Maira Prado, a physiotherapist at the Clinique de Physiothérapie Cabrini, located in Nouveau-Rosemont, believes the interpretation service is not as clear-cut as advertised.
Depuis plus de deux ans, elle travaille: For more than two years, she has volunteered her time to help asylum seekers access the health care system in Quebec. Her passion for the issue has led her to take part in several consultation tables and to compile an <l1>unofficial list of practitioners who provide services to asylum seekers.</l1>
Bien qu’un opérateur du service 811 nous: Although an 811 operator told us that a relative could speak on behalf of an asylum seeker as an interpreter, Maira Prado says this is not always the case. This is because of “the legal barrier, whereby in Quebec, if you are over 14, you must represent yourself before health services.” This means it is not possible to speak on another person’s behalf.
« Le demandeur d’asile doit donc persuad: “So the asylum seeker has to persuade the person on the other end of the phone to accept the interpreter’s help, who may be a friend, an acquaintance or a family member. It is up to that person to show empathy, and that is an important point: the need to raise awareness among all staff who come into contact with asylum seekers,” she stresses.
Au-delà de la langue, M<sup>me </sup>Pra: Beyond language, M<sup>s</sup>. Prado points to other obstacles asylum seekers face that make them, in a way, invisible in the province’s medical records.
« Le problème est que [dans le système t: “The problem is that [in the system as it is designed] they don’t have a health insurance card number (...). That makes access to these patients’ medical information practically impossible,” she explains.
Selon la physiothérapeute, l’absence de: According to the physiotherapist, the lack of a number or of access to patient information largely explains why doctors do not take asylum seekers on as patients. They say, “I don’t know their history, I don’t know anything,” notes M<sup>s</sup>. Prado.
De plus, les demandeurs d’asile ne sont: In addition, asylum seekers are not counted in the health care system. Doctors who see them are paid – it is Blue Cross that pays them – but within the health care system, these consultations are not electronically visible. This “void” prevents doctors from meeting the quotas they must reach to receive government funding.
« Si les médecins d’une clinique voient: “If the doctors in a clinic see asylum seekers all day, it’s as if, in the eyes of the system, they are on vacation,” sums up Maira Prado.
« Nous constatons que les demandeurs d’a: “We see that asylum seekers are penalized many times over. The language barrier is significant, but the systemic barrier must also be denounced,” she adds.
Pour la physiothérapeute, le système don: For the physiotherapist, the system indirectly gives doctors and other health care providers every argument for not taking on asylum seekers. Because, it should be pointed out, signing up to care for them is voluntary.
Selon M<sup>me </sup>Prado, de nombreux: According to M<sup>s</sup>. Prado, many asylum seekers then choose to go to walk-in clinics, but these centres do not give them complete information about the services they are entitled to, she believes. “If it’s a patient who needs musculoskeletal care, for example, walk-in clinic staff don’t mention that there are private clinics that can treat them,” she laments.

Giuliana vit au Canada depuis octobre 20: Giuliana has lived in Canada since October 2022. Originally from Lima, Peru, the 45-year-old woman arrived in Quebec via Roxham Road with her husband and their son, who was three at the time. The family left their home country after a gang extorted monthly payments of $1,000 from them so they could keep their transport business running.
Fernando, leur petit garçon qui a récemm: Fernando, their little boy, who recently turned five, cannot move his right hand properly because of a congenital injury. In Peru, he went to therapy every day to regain his mobility. In Quebec, the situation is very different.
Mère de trois enfants, dont deux sont re: A mother of three, two of whom stayed behind in Peru, Giuliana devotes herself entirely to Fernando, a talkative and affectionate child who calls his injured hand “the champion.” “I work very hard,” he exclaims, laughing.
Malgré ce dévouement, et bien que Giulia: Despite this dedication, and although Giuliana has made progress in integrating into Quebec by taking French-language classes, she only got an appointment with Maira Prado two months ago. Yet these sessions are necessary for Fernando to keep his hand and arm from becoming immobile.
« Il m’a été très difficile d’obtenir le: “It was very hard for me to get the services Fernando needs. First of all, there was the language barrier. It is very hard not to be able to talk to a doctor, not to be able to explain what is going on. On top of his hand injury, we had to go to the emergency room several times for fevers and viruses, and I always have to ask for help,” says Giuliana.
C’est en se tournant vers une organisati: It was by turning to an organization that helps Latin American immigrants that the mother found a solution. “The people at the Centre d’aide aux familles latino-américaines [CAFLA] helped me get appointments. I was very worried because Fernando hadn’t had therapy in more than a year.”
Au CAFLA, Giuliana a reçu l’aide d’un «: At CAFLA, Giuliana received help from an “angel,” she says, visibly relieved. She is talking about Nidia Bravo, an employee of the organization, who helped her find the Clinique de Physiothérapie Cabrini, where she met M<sup>s</sup>. Prado, the physiotherapist Fernando now sees once a week. Communication with her is smooth, because the specialist speaks Spanish.
La recherche de services se poursuit pou: The search for services continues for Giuliana, because Fernando needs a splint for his rehabilitation. Maira Prado is helping her look for it. “I found a certified orthotist who speaks Spanish,” Giuliana says.
« Je ne sais pas encore si nous pourrons: “I don’t know yet whether we’ll be able to get the device for free. I think it costs more than $300, and I’m ready to pay whatever it costs, but we don’t know whether they’ll give us the option of having it made or not,” she adds.
Elle-même a eu du mal à consulter un méd: She herself struggled to see a doctor when she needed one, especially during her first months in Quebec, when her sudden flight from insecurity in Peru weighed on her emotional well-being. “I had a lot of headaches and stomach pain, and I was told it was stress, but for now, I’m waiting to see if a gastroenterologist can see me.”

Chirgwin and others. “The asylum seeker is a patient that no one can see alone.
